title: Can you trust a noisy ruler?
hook: Keep outcomes fixed and change only the accuracy of the horizontal ruler.

knows: arithmetic means, rates and simple plotted values
doesNotKnow: measurement error in the predictor pulls regression slopes toward zero.

misconception: Treating noisy x flattens the slope as valid without checking the stated model, denominators or causal assumptions.
objective: measurement error in the predictor pulls regression slopes toward zero.
keyState: Both finite cases completed; their computed summaries retained.

claims.text: You regress y=2x on x values −2,−1,0,1,2. Add predictor errors 1,−2,2,−2,1. What fitted slope do the noisy x values give?
claims.source: src/demos/probability/p100-noisy-x-flattens-the-slope/spec.ts; exact finite illustration specified in manager numericCase: Latent x [-2,-1,0,1,2], y=2x. Add x-error [1,-2,2,-2,1], orthogonal to x, to obtain observed x [-1,-3,2,-1,3]. Regression slope shrinks from 2 to 20/24=.833333.

claims.text: The noisy ruler retains a slope of 0.833; the exact ruler retains 2. The outcomes stay fixed while the horizontal positions change.
claims.source: src/demos/probability/p100-noisy-x-flattens-the-slope/spec.ts; exact finite illustration specified in manager numericCase: Latent x [-2,-1,0,1,2], y=2x. Add x-error [1,-2,2,-2,1], orthogonal to x, to obtain observed x [-1,-3,2,-1,3]. Regression slope shrinks from 2 to 20/24=.833333.

claims.text: Here the added predictor error is uncorrelated with the true predictor. It increases horizontal variance without adding matching outcome covariance, flattening the fitted slope. Other error structures need not behave this way.
claims.source: src/demos/probability/p100-noisy-x-flattens-the-slope/spec.ts; exact finite illustration specified in manager numericCase: Latent x [-2,-1,0,1,2], y=2x. Add x-error [1,-2,2,-2,1], orthogonal to x, to obtain observed x [-1,-3,2,-1,3]. Regression slope shrinks from 2 to 20/24=.833333.

claims.text: Under independent classical predictor error, extra x variance with unchanged x–y covariance does what to slope? Slope is covariance divided by predictor variance, so adding independent predictor noise attenuates its magnitude.
